newsitem.title: USA: Fed holds rates steady, but for how long?.
newsitem.headline: Fed holds rates steady, but for how long?.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Reserve on Tuesday opted to keep interest rates steady amid overwhelming evidence the world's most powerful economy is growing solidly while inflation is low.

The central bank's widely expected decision not to raise the cost of credit, announced after 3-1/2 hours of closed-door talks, left the key federal funds rate commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans unchanged at 5.5 percent.
Financial markets took the news in their stride. The Dow Jones industrial average continued its recovery from last week's steep losses and closed the day 114.74 points higher at 7,918.10.

With recent data painting a picture of an economy humming along comfortably without hitting any inflationary bumps, analysts saw little reason for the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) to do anything but keep its powder dry.

Investors' attention immediately turned to the next rate meetings, as many are convinced the central bank will move to tighten credit later in the year as faster growth raises the specter of higher inflation. The next FOMC meetings are set for Sept. 30 and Nov. 12.

"There's a 50-50 chance that the Fed could hike interest rates in September and probably a better than a 50-50 chance of a move on Nov. 12. There are a number of reasons, the primary one being economic growth," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Corp. in Minneapolis.
The Fed last bumped up interest rates in March when it raised the federal funds rate by a quarter percentage point in a preemptive bid to choke off inflation pressures.

At its subsequent meetings in May and June the FOMC decided to stand by, reportedly nudged along by Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan who convinced fellow policy makers that the economy would lose some of its steam if left to itself.
Just last month, Greenspan told lawmakers that the Fed was prepared to raise rates if needed to squelch inflation but suggested that might not happen anytime soon.

Economic growth dipped to 2.2 percent in the second quarter of the year from its breakneck pace of 4.9 percent in the January-March period as consumers' spending spree fizzled out and unsold inventories began to build up.

Consumer prices so far this year have increased at their slowest pace in 11 years and producer prices in July dropped for an record seventh month in a row. Real wages have declined even though the U.S. labor market remains tight, with the unemployment hovering at a 24-year low.
Higher interest rates would have made borrowing more expensive and put a damper on economic activity by reducing consumers' and companies' ability to spend and invest.

That could be exactly what the Fed may want to do sometime later this year or early in 1998, most analysts say. Three more meetings before the end of this year would give the FOMC plenty of opportunity to revise its policy stance.
If growth should pick up from its second-quarter lull at a rate that worried policy makers, they may well be prompted to hit the brakes before the damage shows in inflation numbers.

"The odds favor that there will be a tightening at some point. It's a tough call ... but I would say it slightly favors fourth quarter still," said William Dudley, chief economist at Wall Street broker Goldman, Sachs & Co. Inc.

The Fed is expected to keep a particularly close watch on a tentative agreement to end the 15-day strike by the Teamsters union against United Parcel Service, widely seen as a victory for U.S. organized labor.

Analysts have warned that sweeping concessions by the nation's biggest package delivery company could feed through into upward pressure on wages in other parts of the economy, potentially fueling inflation down the road.
